title: Inference Operating Agreement (one-pager)
content:
Context: Draft internal one-pager meant to reframe Redwood's core positioning as an operating contract for teams shipping LLM features. Target audience: platform leads, engineering managers, and solution architects evaluating tradeoffs between building inference in-house vs. adopting Redwood. Tone: pragmatic, contractual, developer-focused — fewer marketing metaphors, more concrete guarantees and tradeoffs.

Problem statement:
- Teams building LLM features face three recurring operational failures: unpredictable unit costs, silent quality regressions after model/infra changes, and emergent latencies under load that break UX flows.
- These failures show up as surprise infra spend, missed SLIs, and long rollback windows that disrupt product roadmaps.

The Redwood promise (one-line operating contract):
- We commit to make inference behave like a first-class platform service — predictable cost per active user, bounded tail latency, and upgrade-safe rollouts — so product teams can ship LLM features without building a bespoke inference org.

Core clauses (how we operationalize the promise):
1) Economic SLOs: "Unit economics guarantee"
   - Outcome: Customers get a clear, predictable per-1000-token cost profile for a given workload class (chat, single-turn generate, embeddings) with documented tails and burst pricing policies.
   - Why it matters: Teams can model feature ROI and decide whether an LLM feature is viable before full launch.

2) Latency envelope and fallbacks: "Bounded latency guarantee"
   - Outcome: 95th/99th token latency SLOs per deployment tier; automated fallback routing to compatible model variant when SLOs are at risk.
   - Why it matters: UX-critical flows (search augmentation, chat) keep service-level latencies even under transient contention.

3) Upgrade safety and observable regressions: "Release contract"
   - Outcome: Canary rollouts with automatic quality regression detection against customer-provided prompt suites; automatic rollback triggers and postmortem hooks.
   - Why it matters: Avoids the common issue of silent quality drift when models or quantization profiles change.

4) Data & control boundaries: "Operational custody"
   - Outcome: Clear modes (hosted, dedicated, private) with explicit data residency, KMS integration, and audit logs. Customers pick the custody that matches regulatory and legal constraints while preserving the same API semantics.
   - Why it matters: Keeps compliance and network policy decisions orthogonal to developer experience.

5) Cost controls and runbook primitives: "Economic guardrails"
   - Outcome: Token budgets, route-level throttles, cache/aggregation recommendations surfaced by our optimizer, and per-route cost breakdowns in the console.
   - Why it matters: Prevents rogue features from generating unbounded spend while enabling safe experimentation.

Differentiators vs. common alternatives (short):
- Building in-house: You get custom control but pay months/years of ops toil to match cost-efficiency and rollout safety; probability of achieving comparable observability and fallback automation is low without large dedicated teams.
- Cloud-managed endpoints (generic): They expose low-level infra but rarely provide workload-aware economics or automatic quality regression detection — that is, they solve infrastructure but not predictable product delivery.
- Other inference vendors: Many emphasize raw throughput or model access; Redwood packages throughput with operating guarantees (economics + safety + observability) targeted at product delivery.

Customer outcomes (metrics we help achieve):
- Reduce median rollout time for model/quantization upgrades from weeks to days (metric: mean time to safe rollout).
- Cut per-feature inference cost variance by 40% by adding batching, caching, and routing policies (metric: coefficient of variation of cost per 1k tokens across a month).
- Achieve targeted 99th-token latency SLOs for customer-critical routes under 95% of sustained traffic peaks (metric: % of peaks where SLOs maintained).

Tactical messaging hooks (for docs/SDRs/AE):
- Elevator: "Redwood turns inference into an operating contract: predictable cost, bounded latency, and upgrade-safe rollouts so your product roadmap doesn't hinge on an ops team."
- For platform leads: "Give your teams a stable inference surface — same API across hosted/dedicated/private, plus observable guardrails that make cost and quality predictable."
- For engineering managers: "Ship LLM features without creating a second ops org — we handle the economics, fallbacks, and rollout safety that usually cause surprise pages and spiraling costs."

Evidence & proof points to include in collateral (short list):
- Case study stub: mid-market SaaS reduced query cost variance by 45% after enabling caching + policy routing. (private notes: anonymized metrics available in GM-4123)
- Technical brief: Canary regression detection architecture and sample prompt-suite integration (link: confluence:INF-ops-contracts-2025).
- Benchmarks: tail latency vs. model variants under mixed workloads (internal benchmark PR: github:repo/fast-rollout-pr-78).

Open questions & assumptions (workshopping section):
- How prescriptive should our default economic SLOs be vs. recommending ranges? (assume: start with conservative defaults, let customers opt into aggressive optimization).
- Which triggers should force an automatic rollback vs. notify-only? (assume: severe quality regression or SLO breach = auto rollback; minor drift = notify).
- Pricing signal integration: how to show projected monthly spend impact of enabling optimizer suggestions in-console? (work with finance/product).

Next steps (owner + timeline):
- Draft canonical one-pager for public-facing site (owner: Ava; due: 2025-02-28).
- Build a short tech appendix showing canary/regression detection flow (owner: Liam; due: 2025-03-07).
- Prepare two slide templates: platform-lead brief and engineering-manager brief (owner: Maya; due: 2025-03-03).

Notes to self / rough language to preserve in final edit:
- Avoid abstract 'trust' metaphors; use concrete guarantees and measurable outcomes.
- Lead with the economics clause when speaking to GTM — ROI modeling is the gate for most product teams.

Slack refs: #go-to-market-inference (thread: March product-sell-in), #engineering-ops (thread: canary-rollback-patterns).

Draft status: rough — ready for quick sync with product + SRE to align on rollback semantics and the minimum viable set of SLOs we can publish.
